panels.title: Waiting
panels.description: Accepted, not started. This is the number a visitor is behind in the queue.

panels.title: Rendering
panels.description: One at a time by design: MAX_CONCURRENT_RENDERS is 1, and prefetch=1 on the broker enforces it. Two here would mean two consumers.

panels.title: Delivered
panels.description: Counted when the video exists, never at submission.

panels.title: Failed
panels.description: Jobs that ended in an error and were not retried. A render that fails on its inputs fails the same way again, so it is reported rather than requeued.

panels.title: Realtime factor
panels.description: Seconds of work per second of music. Every queue estimate rests on this. Measured 1.29 on two shared cores; below 1.0 means faster than realtime.

panels.title: Peak memory ever
panels.description: The largest a render has grown on this host. The bar is what the box has: red means a render has come within reach of the machine's limit, which ends as a killed worker, not a slow one.

panels.title: Memory headroom
panels.description: The only graph on this dashboard that predicts an outage rather than describing one. `Used` is total minus MemAvailable - the kernel's own estimate of what a new allocation can actually get, which is the question being asked; MemFree would count the page cache as a crisis. The ceiling is this box's RAM, and the dashed line is where the alert fires. `Highest a render has reached` is our own high-water mark, recorded by the worker in the events it already sends - so it survives the machine that produced it, which matters once the renderer moves to a host that is destroyed after each job. Measured so far: 2457 MB on a 7.1-minute recording, on a 3915 MB box. The upload cap is 8 minutes - lowered from 25 because 14.1 minutes measured 4.62 GB against 3915 MB and OOM-killed the box - and `align` is DTW - its cost is the product of the two sequence lengths, so it grows with the SQUARE of duration. Watch this as longer uploads arrive: the shape of the peak line against recording length is what sizes the compute node.  A LIMIT OF THIS PANEL, measured: `align` allocated 2433 MB in 18.6 seconds on a 7.1-minute recording. Prometheus scrapes every 30s, so the blue `Used` line can miss that spike entirely - during the test render it sampled a peak of 2021 MB while the process tree actually reached 2433 MB. The red line does not have this problem: it comes from getrusage in the worker, is exact, and is what to trust for sizing. `Used` is a floor, not a ceiling.

targets.legendFormat: Highest a render has ever reached

matcher.options: Highest a render has ever reached

panels.title: Would a machine be up
panels.description: NOTHING HERE CREATES A MACHINE. Every scrape records what a scaler would have decided, so the trigger can be judged against real traffic before it is given the power to spend money. 1 means a node would exist; 0 means none would. Compare it against the queue below: a band of 1 with no work under it is the grace period doing its job, and a band that never returns to 0 means the grace period is longer than the gaps between jobs - at which point scale-to-zero is buying nothing and a permanent machine would be cheaper.

panels.title: The queue, and the idle clock
panels.description: How long there has been no work at all, against the grace period it is judged by. THIS IS THE PANEL THAT SETS COMPUTE_GRACE_SECONDS. Every time the idle line crosses the dashed one, a machine is torn down; if work then arrives shortly after, that teardown cost the next visitor a ~2 minute wait for a new boot and cost you the creation. Watch how often the gaps between jobs are shorter than the line: if they usually are, raise the grace period; if the line is almost never reached, lower it and stop paying for idle.

panels.title: Why it would start and stop
panels.description: The reason, which Prometheus cannot hold - a distinct message per decision would be a new series each time, so the counts live in Prometheus and the why comes straight from the app. Each row is one decision the scaler would have taken, with the queue depth and idle time it saw at that moment. Read it next to the graphs above when a band starts or ends and the reason is not obvious.

panels.title: What it would have cost
panels.description: Machine-hours a scaler would have run over the selected window, and what that is in money at the configured plan rate. THIS IS THE NUMBER THE WHOLE SCALE-TO-ZERO DESIGN EXISTS TO MAKE SMALL - and the one to compare against a permanently-running instance before committing to the complexity. If it approaches the cost of leaving a machine up, the simpler thing is also the cheaper thing.

panels.title: What is the limiting factor
panels.description: Every resource as a percentage of itself, so the highest line IS the bottleneck - that is the whole point of this panel, and why the units are normalised rather than native. Measured during a real render of the Op. 39 Scherzo: CPU 98%, memory 34%, disk 0.1%, iowait 0.01% - so at encode the answer is CPU, and only CPU. At `align` it is memory instead: 2457 MB of 3915 on a 7.1-minute recording. The bottleneck MOVES between stages, which is why this panel is a time series and not a gauge. Read it during a render: if CPU is at 95% and everything else is low, a faster processor is the upgrade; if disk-busy is on top, a faster CPU buys nothing. TWO OF THESE CANNOT BE MEASURED FROM INSIDE A VIRTUAL MACHINE. Memory BANDWIDTH needs CPU performance counters, which a Linode guest is not given - if memory speed is ever the suspect it has to be settled by a benchmark on the box, not by this dashboard. CPU CLOCK SPEED is fixed and invisible for the same reason; what you can see instead is `steal` on the panel below, which is the hypervisor handing our slice to somebody else - the honest measure of not getting the CPU we paid for. Network is drawn in absolute terms further down: the link ceiling is not reported by the machine, so a percentage would be invented.

panels.title: CPU load against cores
panels.description: Load average is a count of processes wanting to run, so it means nothing without the core count - which is drawn here rather than left for you to remember. Below the line the machine keeps up; above it, work is queuing and every render runs slower than its estimate. Unlike memory this is not fatal: a saturated CPU makes the site slow, it does not get anything killed. If 1 min sits above 15 min the load is still climbing. Encode is 92% of a job and uses 1.92 of the 2 cores here, so during a render this is MEANT to sit near the line - what matters is whether it comes back down afterwards.

panels.title: Where the CPU actually goes
panels.description: Busy-ness split by what it is busy with, stacked against the whole machine. READ `nice` FIRST: vsw-worker.service sets Nice=5, so the render's own CPU - ffmpeg, measured at 182% of 2 cores - lands there and NOT in `user`. During a render `nice` is around 90% and `user` about 6%; taking `user` as the workload would tell you the box was idle while it was in fact 98% consumed. `user` here is the web app, Grafana and Prometheus. `iowait` is the processor stalled on a disk - tall iowait during encode would mean the disk is the limit and a faster CPU would buy nothing; measured at 0.01%, so it is not. `steal` is time the hypervisor gave to another tenant on the same physical host: not our load, not fixable by us, and a persistent few percent is the argument for a dedicated-CPU plan. Measured at 0.01% here, so this shared plan is currently delivering what it promises - and it is the closest this stack can get to measuring CPU speed.

targets.expr: sum by (mode) (rate(node_cpu_seconds_total{mode!="idle"}[5m])) / on() group_left count(count by (cpu) (node_cpu_seconds_total{mode="idle"}))

panels.title: Disk, and whether it is the limit
panels.description: `Busy` is the fraction of time the device had a request outstanding - utilisation, not throughput, and the number that says whether the disk is the constraint. Near 100% with modest MB/s means seeks, not bandwidth. The throughput lines matter because this pipeline is unusually file-heavy: a 131 MB output, its uploaded source, and the extracted audio all cross this device, and uploads are KEPT rather than swept.

panels.title: Network throughput
panels.description: In absolute bytes per second, not as a percentage: the machine does not report its link ceiling, so any percentage here would be a number we made up. Judge it against the plan - and against the fact that a finished video is ~131 MB, so a handful of simultaneous downloads is the realistic load, not the renders themselves. `lo` is excluded; it is Prometheus scraping this box and would swamp the real traffic.

panels.title: Stage of the job in flight
panels.description: Which stage the running job is in, over time. A flat line at one stage for longer than usual is the first sign of trouble, and encode is legitimately about nine tenths of a render.

panels.title: Share of a job's time, by stage
panels.description: Averaged over the window, not over all history. Encode dominating is expected; anything else dominating is the finding.

panels.title: Cores used, by stage
panels.description: CPU seconds divided by wall seconds: how many cores a stage really occupies. Approaching the core count means the box is the limit and a bigger one would help almost linearly; well below it means the stage is waiting on something else.

panels.title: Memory high-water, by stage
panels.description: The peak reached by the end of each stage. Cumulative for the process, so the RISE from one stage to the next is what that stage cost. Alignment is the one that grows with the SQUARE of the recording's length.

panels.title: Seconds of work per gigabyte uploaded
panels.description: The figure the caps were set from. Length is what actually costs — the canvas is a fixed 1080p whatever arrives — so this drifts with the kind of video people send, and is worth watching rather than trusting.

panels.title: Failures, by the stage they happened in
panels.description: Empty is the expected state. Which stage a failure lands in says what to look at: align is the recording, bands is the score package, encode is ffmpeg or the machine.

panels.title: Why the failures failed
panels.description: The reason, not the count. Prometheus cannot hold this — an error message as a label is one new series per distinct failure — so it comes straight from the app. The command is the ffmpeg line that was actually run, assembled from what the visitor chose; paste it into a terminal to reproduce.

panels.title: Who is using this, and from where
Where the uploads come from
panels.description: The server-location answer, and the one to read first. Built from the country recorded at the time of each upload, not from re-resolving addresses now - so it survives a recording being deleted, and a block of addresses being reassigned cannot rewrite last year. Sorted by minutes of video, because that is what has to cross an ocean.

panels.title: What people actually play
panels.description: Every piece the recogniser has named here. 'Asked' counts answers and 'Uploads' counts recordings - a visitor who asked twice about one video is 2 and 1. Length is a median with its range, never a mean: one thirty-second test upload of a twenty-minute Ballade would drag an average somewhere neither figure has ever been. 'Confidence' is the winner's share of the whole ranked list, so a low one means the runners-up were close, not that the answer was wrong.

panels.title: Every visitor, by address
panels.description: One row per internet address, with the city it resolves to. There is no login here, so this is the only thing that distinguishes one visitor from another, and it is what the daily upload limit is counted against. It is deleted with the recording when somebody asks - which is why the two tables above are built from the recorded country instead, and go on working afterwards.

panels.title: Every answer the recogniser gave
panels.description: The rows the two tables above are built from, newest first - where an implausible median or an unexpected country comes from. Deliberately carries no address: the job id is here instead, and the address is reached by looking that job up while it still exists. 'Consensus' is how much of the recording agreed with itself, over how many windows; a high confidence over two windows is arithmetic, not evidence.
